name: PT Supra Boga Lestari Tbk

frontmatter.title: Supra Boga Lestari: premium stores, premium rent, thin equity
frontmatter.summary: RANC runs Indonesia's premium supermarket banners under Blibli. Sales are growing but the estate is smaller, and the rent is charged once, in capex, with the lease liability outside the valuation bridge. The most likely path values the equity at a fraction of the price: margins are thin and the renewal bill is heavy. The target is probability-weighted and bull-dominated; the rating rests on the base case. SELL.
thesis: The equity is a thin residual: EBITDA of IDR178.6bn less IDR165.1bn of D&A and IDR194.0bn of lease-inclusive capex leaves FCFF of IDR-18.2bn in the investment year [S4][S0].

One lease convention runs through the valuation: the right-of-use renewals are charged in capex, so FCFF is post-rent, and the lease liability of IDR301.7bn is added back in the equity bridge rather than deducted twice; the DCF then values the equity at Rp72 per share on an enterprise value of IDR181.4bn [S4][S0].
The market pays 3.2x book and 6.5x EBITDA for a business with a return on equity of -7.4% and no dividend [S0][S4].

The most likely path values the equity at Rp93; the published target of Rp111 is the probability-weighted value of Rp159 after a 30.0% liquidity discount, and the bull scenario at Rp1,074 on a 10% weight supplies most of it. The SELL rests on the base case, not on the tail [S0].
The 9 December 2026 EGM on alcohol retail, cold storage and pharmaceutical wholesale is real optionality, but it is an approval, not an asset, and we keep it only in the bull case [S3].

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp111 (-77.8% total return), against a share price of Rp500. The most likely path values the equity at Rp93.** RANC operates premium supermarkets in a market where the rent for the stores is larger than the profit from the shelves. That is not a temporary condition: in FY2025 the group earned EBITDA of IDR147.7bn and paid IDR31.6bn of finance cost, most of it lease interest, while committing IDR100.2bn to new right-of-use assets and IDR36.9bn to owned fixed assets, and paying IDR131.2bn of lease liabilities and IDR26.0bn of lease interest in cash [S4]. We charge the rent once: the right-of-use renewals sit in capex, so free cash flow to the firm of IDR-18.2bn in our first forecast year is already post-rent, and the lease liability is kept out of the equity bridge [S4][S0]. The alternative convention — lease liabilities as debt with the renewals excluded from capex — is set out in the valuation section below; run correctly it gives broadly the same equity value, because the present value of the renewal stream is what the lease liability measures [S4].

The operating story has genuinely improved. Revenue fell in FY2023, recovered in FY2024 and reached IDR2,914.5bn in FY2025, and the nine months to September 2026 grew faster than the full prior year as the estate stopped shrinking and the remaining stores traded better [S4][S0]. Management closed the weakest outlets, ending FY2025 with 57 stores against 60 a year earlier, and says explicitly that it is prioritising quality over count [S4]. The FY2026 target set in the annual report is revenue of IDR3,390.0bn and operating profit of IDR23.3bn [S4]. We do not adopt either. The revenue target needs a pace the nine-month run-rate does not show, and the profit target needs an operating margin well above the nine-month actual, which would require a fourth-quarter operating margin far above the nine-month average. We carry 10.0% for FY2026E and an operating profit of IDR13.5bn, which is the nine-month cumulative plus one more quarter at the nine-month average, with no seasonal uplift assumed [S0][S4].

The variant view is about the equity, not the stores. A premium grocer can be a good business and a bad stock if the rent and the capital intensity absorb the cash, and that is what the corrected cash flow says. The DCF is now positive rather than floored: an enterprise value of IDR181.4bn against the interim net debt the valuation bridge uses, with the lease liability of IDR301.7bn added back because the rent is already in capex, gives equity of Rp72 per share [S0][S4]. The base-case blend is Rp82 — the DCF at 98% weight, with P/BV at Rp415 and EV/sales at Rp688 carried at 1% each — which rolls at the cost of equity to the most likely value of Rp93 [S0]. The published target is not that number. It is the probability-weighted value of Rp159 across Rp12, Rp93 and Rp1,074 at 40.0%, 50.0% and 10.0% — less the 30.0% liquidity discount, which gives Rp111 [S0]. The bull case carries most of that weighted value: its 10% weight times Rp1,074 is larger than the base case's 50% weight times Rp93. The SELL does not rest on that tail. It rests on the most likely path: the base case of Rp93 is below the published target of Rp111 and both are far below the share price, so the direction is the same whichever number the reader takes [S0].

What the market is paying for is a recovery we cannot source. At Rp500 the market pays 6.5x EBITDA and 3.2x book for a group whose return on equity is -7.4% and which has paid no dividend for two years [S0][S4]. Running the model backwards does not produce a growth rate that reaches the price: the solver adds its factor to every forecast year, and even an implausibly large addition to every year's revenue growth leaves the DCF value below Rp500 [S0]. The gap is a margin-and-rent gap, not a growth gap. A re-rating is possible — the 9 December EGM could add higher-margin wholesale and specialty lines, and the Blibli ecosystem gives the banners traffic that standalone grocers do not have [S3] — but an approval is not an asset. We keep that optionality in the bull case and out of the base case.

Three things move the value: the gross margin, which at 24.9% is decent for grocery but not enough to carry an opex bill of IDR739.1bn; the rent, where the right-of-use renewals plus lease interest together consume most of EBITDA; and the sales recovery, which is real but is coming from a smaller store base. The first two are structural, the third is cyclical. Both the most likely value and the published target are below the current price because the thin margin leaves little for the equity after the rent and the debt service — not because we have adopted a bearish path.

RANC is an Indonesian supermarket operator focused on the premium and upper-middle segment. At the end of FY2025 it operated 57 outlets, down from 60 a year earlier, of which 16 traded under the Ranch Market banner and 36 under Farmers Market, with the balance in the smaller specialty formats the group also runs [S4]. Ranch Market is the premium end — imported and fresh lines, a large prepared-food and bakery offer — while Farmers Market is the larger, mid-premium format that carries most of the store count. The group employed 2,716 people including its subsidiary PT Supra Mas Mandiri at the end of FY2025 [S4].

The company reports two geographic segments and no brand-level profit and loss. The West Area covers Jakarta and its surroundings plus Sumatra; the East Area covers East Java, Central Java, Kalimantan and Maluku [S4]. The accounts disclose revenue and operating result by those two regions only, so the brand mix has to be inferred from the store counts rather than read from a segment table. That is a disclosure limitation worth stating plainly: an investor cannot see from the filings whether Ranch Market or Farmers Market earns the group margin, and the group does not publish same-store sales by banner.

The business model is conventional premium grocery: buy through a central procurement and distribution operation, assemble a differentiated assortment that includes imported and private-label lines, and sell it through stores whose locations and leases are the scarce resource. The difference from a mass-format retailer is that the premium basket supports a higher gross margin but a smaller addressable market, and the locations that support it are expensive. The group also sells online through merchant agreements with PT Global Digital Niaga Tbk (Blibli), a related party, and with HappyFresh and GrabMart, which gives it a delivery channel without owning the last mile [S4]. That channel matters strategically because the controlling shareholder also controls the platform.

Ownership is concentrated. Blibli held 70.6% of the shares at the end of FY2025, with two other named shareholders, PT Prima Rasa Inti and PT Wijaya Sumber Sejahtera, holding the rest alongside the public at 11.8% [S4]. The market data put the free float at 11.7% [S0]; the difference from the annual report's public figure is definitional, because the report's public holding includes small strategic holders. The company is therefore part of the Djarum group's retail and digital complex, with Blibli as parent, platform and related-party supplier of traffic. We treat that as a governance feature rather than a flaw: it gives the banners a distribution and data partner that peers lack, but it also means the minority sits behind a controlling shareholder's capital-allocation priorities, and the free float is thin enough to matter for liquidity (see the governance section).

The strategy since the 2025 restructuring has been to shrink into strength. Management closed outlets it judged no longer viable, kept the better leases, and redirected investment into refreshing the remaining estate; it describes the priority as outlet quality rather than outlet count [S4]. The next step is diversification without new stores. On 2 November 2026 the company announced that it will ask shareholders at an extraordinary general meeting on 9 December 2026 to approve new business lines: retail sale of alcoholic beverages, warehousing and other storage including cold storage, and wholesale of pharmaceutical products for human use [S3]. The rationale given is to use the existing store network, storage and distribution system to earn third-party storage revenue, widen the assortment, and centralise pharmaceutical procurement for the stores [S3]. If approved, these are adjacent businesses with different licences and different margin structures; they are not yet revenue. The infrastructure the company would use is already inside the store estate's fixed-asset and right-of-use base, so there is no separately disclosed cold-storage asset to value; we keep the new lines out of the base case and let their contribution sit in the bull case, where it is part of the margin shock [S3][S4].

Indonesian premium grocery sits between two worlds. On one side are the traditional wet markets and the small independent shops that still sell most of the country's food, where freshness and price are set daily and credit is informal. On the other are the modern-format chains, which brought air-conditioning, fixed prices, imported lines and loyalty programmes to the middle class. The premium end of the modern trade grew with the shopping-mall culture of the large cities and with a segment of households that treats food shopping as leisure as much as provisioning. That segment is small, cyclical and sensitive to confidence, which is why premium grocers tend to have a handful of flagships in the best malls and a long tail of neighbourhood stores that must earn their rent. The format also carries a service-heavy cost base — butchers, bakers, deli counters, prepared food — that a discount chain does not. In a downturn, the premium banner is the first place a household trades down from, and the last place it trades back to.

The demand backdrop is stable rather than buoyant. Indonesia grew 5.1% in FY2025 and 5.5% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, and consumer price inflation was 3.2% in October 2026 [S4][S8][S7]. Household consumption grew 2.6% in 2025, and the company itself notes that the growth was uneven and concentrated in the upper-middle segment that it targets [S2]. That is the key industry fact for RANC: the premium grocery market is a narrow slice of a large and growing consumption economy, and its growth depends more on the confidence of the top income deciles than on the aggregate GDP number. A mid-single-digit economy with low-single-digit inflation gives a food retailer a modest nominal tailwind; it does not give a premium format a volume tailwind unless the top decile is doing better than the average, which the company says it is [S2].

Competition is intense at both ends of the market. In mass grocery the large minimarket and supermarket chains compete on price, store density and supply chain, and they have the scale to absorb thin margins. In premium grocery RANC competes with the food halls attached to department stores, with independent premium and organic retailers, and increasingly with the e-grocery platforms that deliver the same imported and fresh assortment without a store visit. The company's own online route runs through Blibli, HappyFresh and GrabMart, so it participates in that substitution rather than being purely a victim of it [S4]. We do not have a reliable public market-share number for the premium segment; the group does not disclose one, and the available industry data does not separate premium grocery from the modern trade as a whole. We therefore treat RANC as a challenger with a recognised brand rather than a share leader, and we do not build a share-gain assumption into the base case.

Regulation cuts both ways. The new business lines need shareholder approval and then licences: alcohol retail is restricted and politically sensitive in Indonesia, pharmaceutical wholesale requires a distribution licence, and cold storage and warehousing carry their own permits and food-safety rules [S3]. Approval at the EGM is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one, and the timing of revenue from any of the three lines is uncertain. On the core business, retail licensing, labour rules and the treatment of lease contracts are the relevant constraints, and none of them is changing in a way that we can source as a material swing factor for FY2026E or FY2027E [S4].

The moat is real but narrow. The brand is known in its segment, the fresh and prepared-food offer is hard to replicate in a minimarket, and the Blibli relationship gives the group a digital shopfront and customer data that a family-owned premium grocer would have to build. Against that, switching costs for a shopper are close to zero, the premium assortment is available from competitors and from the platforms, and the critical scarce input — a good lease in a good location — is won at auction against other retailers. The five forces therefore read: high buyer power, high rivalry, moderate supplier power (fresh and imported supply is fragmented but quality-constrained), moderate threat of new entrants (capital and licences, but the format is replicable), and high threat of substitutes from traditional trade and delivery. That is a structure in which a well-run operator earns a modest return on capital and a badly run one earns nothing. RANC's margins say it is in the second group today and trying to move to the first [S4].

The external influences we watch are food inflation, the rupiah and wages. Food inflation drives the cost of the fresh and imported basket and the shopper's willingness to pay a premium for it; the rupiah matters for imported lines and for the dollar-denominated part of the supply chain; and wages matter because the format is service-heavy and the minimum wage is set administratively. The macro deck's balance-of-payments pressure and cautious consumer stance is consistent with our view that the premium segment grows, but slowly, and that pricing power is limited [S7][S8].

Grocery retail is a scale business with a local moat. Distribution centres, procurement terms and private-label development all improve with volume, but the customer chooses the store she can reach, so the network matters more than the national share. That is why the large chains expand store by store and why a premium operator can survive in a handful of wealthy catchments without ever being the biggest. The competitive dynamic in the premium niche is less about price than about assortment and experience: the shopper who buys imported cheese and fresh salmon is not comparing shelf prices with the minimarket down the road. The weakness of the model is that this shopper is also the most mobile and the most exposed to confidence shocks, and the landlord knows it. Rents in the best malls are set by the tenant mix, not by the grocer's margin, so a premium retailer that loses its edge cannot simply renegotiate. The format's history in the region is one of long leases signed in good years and renegotiated in bad ones.

Revenue has been flat for four years in nominal terms, which in a country with positive inflation means it has shrunk in real terms. The group reported IDR2,898.8bn in FY2022, IDR2,804.2bn in FY2023, IDR2,874.1bn in FY2024 and IDR2,914.5bn in FY2025 [S4]. The gross margin improved over the same period, from 23.2% to 24.9%, as the mix moved toward fresh and prepared food and the closed stores stopped dragging [S4]. That improvement is the single most important operating fact in the file: the remaining estate earns a better margin than the estate that included the closed outlets.

The cost base did not fall as fast as the revenue base. Opex was IDR722.8bn in FY2022 and IDR739.1bn in FY2025, so the operating result went from IDR-50.7bn to IDR-73.8bn to IDR-37.0bn to IDR-14.7bn [S4]. The reported loss from operations in the LK is larger — IDR-26.7bn — because it includes other operating expenses, principally losses on asset disposals and right-of-use impairments, that we treat as non-recurring [S4]. We use the data pack's operating line for history because it is the comparable series to the nine-month 2026 accounts, which show a positive operating result for the first time in three years [S0]. The gap between the two definitions is a classification judgement, not a data error; we state it because a reader comparing our table with the LK will see it.

The bottom line is worse than the operating line because of finance costs. Net finance expense was IDR31.6bn in FY2025, down from IDR41.8bn as the group repaid bank lines, but it still exceeds operating profit [S4]. The result was a loss attributable to shareholders of IDR-53.1bn, after a profit of IDR27.4bn in FY2024 that came from a one-off gain on the disposal of an associate rather than from retailing [S4]. The only recent year of reported profit is therefore not evidence of earning power, and we do not extrapolate it.

The nine months to September 2026 are the first genuine evidence of a turnaround, but the quarterly path matters. The data pack's quarterly accounts show a strongly positive first quarter, a loss-making second quarter in which gross margin fell and the opex ratio rose, and a return to operating profit in the third; the nine-month cumulative operating result is positive only because the first quarter was large enough to absorb the second [S0]. The nine-month figures are derived from the data pack's quarterly block because the first- and third-quarter filing archives are not machine-readable, and we say so rather than present them as filing quotes [S0][S5][S9]. We carry the cumulative into FY2026E: revenue of IDR3,206.0bn, a gross margin of 24.9% and an operating profit of IDR13.5bn [S0][S4]. The operating profit sits above the nine-month cumulative only because we add one more quarter at the nine-month average: FY2026E EBIT is the nine-month result plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month run-rate, with no seasonal uplift assumed. The model holds the nine-month opex ratio, so the implied fourth-quarter operating profit is close to the nine-month quarterly average, and the bridge adds a normal quarter rather than a festive one. That is why we do not use the company's own operating-profit target of IDR23.3bn. Reaching that target would require a fourth-quarter margin far above anything the first nine months show, and the target was set before the second-quarter squeeze was visible [S4][S0]. The FY2025 target was also missed, and the estate is smaller, so the nine-month run-rate is the better guide than a target set before the year began [S4][S2].

Beyond FY2026E the forecast is a slow normalisation. Revenue grows 6.0% in FY2027E and fades to 4.0% by FY2030E, which is roughly inflation plus a small real gain from a flat store base [S7]. The gross margin holds near 25.1% and the opex ratio falls to 24.3%, giving an operating margin of 0.8% by FY2030E [S4]. That is still a thin margin for a retailer, and it is the reason the equity value is low: at IDR224.9bn of EBITDA and IDR193.9bn of lease-inclusive capex, the business is only just covering its cost of capital. The bottom line does not turn positive within the horizon: finance costs of IDR36.9bn absorb the operating result, and net profit to parent is IDR-5.7bn in FY2030E because the lease and bank debt are refinanced rather than repaid [S4][S0].

Capex is the line that decides the valuation, and the table needs a word of explanation because it mixes bases. The historical line is the data pack's cash investing outflow, IDR45.2bn in FY2025 [S0]. The accrual, lease-inclusive build is owned fixed-asset additions of IDR36.9bn plus right-of-use additions through new lease liabilities of IDR100.2bn for FY2025, and IDR36.2bn plus IDR136.0bn for FY2024 [S4]. We charge the rent here, once: because the right-of-use renewals are a capex line, the lease liability is excluded from the valuation bridge below, and the same convention then runs through every scenario. The consequence is that the table's historical FCFF of IDR62.3bn is on the data pack's cash basis and is not comparable with the forecast: on the lease-inclusive basis the same year's FCFF is lower by the right-of-use additions of IDR100.2bn. Our forecast capex is IDR194.0bn in FY2026E, an investment year in which the nine-month cash outflow already exceeded the whole of FY2025, falling to 5.0% of revenue by FY2030E and rising to 5.2% thereafter, above D&A of 5.0%, so the estate replaces its fixed-asset and lease base as it grows [S0][S4]. Two cash facts set the FY2026E rate of 6.0%: the renewal proxy understates the rent, because FY2025 lease payments were IDR131.2bn plus IDR26.0bn of lease interest against IDR100.2bn of right-of-use additions; and the model's cash roll has to end the year above the 30 September interim net debt, which at the old rate it did not [S4][S0]. The FY2026E D&A ratio of 5.1% is set at the nine-month 2026 actual and held flat through the fourth quarter; we do not step it up to the FY2025 full-year ratio. The FY2025 fourth quarter did carry a slightly higher depreciation charge than its third quarter, but one quarter is not a seasonality we can source into FY2026E, so the fourth-quarter D&A uses the same ratio as the first nine months. We fade the ratio to 5.0% as the older right-of-use assets run off [S0].

The tax line needs the same care. The balance sheet carries accumulated fiscal losses of IDR216.6bn at the end of FY2025, split between the 2022, 2023 and 2025 loss years, and Indonesian law allows a five-year carry-forward [S4]. The forecast EBIT through FY2030E is smaller than the available losses, so no cash tax is paid in the explicit years; the losses expire between 2027 and 2030, and from FY2031E the statutory rate applies to FCFF. We do not treat the deferred-tax asset on the balance sheet as an extra cash shield [S4].

Working capital is small and supplier-funded. Operating working capital was IDR26.1bn, or 0.9% of revenue, and we hold that ratio through the forecast [S4]. The FY2025 working-capital swing of IDR41.1bn was large and is one reason reported FCFF in that year looks better than the underlying cash generation; it does not repeat in the forecast [S0].

The balance sheet is the constraint. At the end of FY2025 the group had IDR77.6bn of cash, IDR401.7bn of gross debt, dominated by the lease liability, and equity of IDR263.4bn [S4]. Net debt was IDR324.1bn, or 2.2 EBITDA, and it rises to IDR374.6bn in FY2026E, above the 30 September 2026 interim balance the valuation bridge uses, because the year's operating cash does not cover the rent and the renewal capex [S4][S0]. The FY2026E roll starts from that interim balance sheet: the year carries the actual drawdown of gross debt to the 30 September figure and no further net borrowing is assumed beyond it [S0]. Equity falls to IDR244.5bn and then to IDR211.8bn before the cumulative losses stop; there is no dividend and no buyback to support the per-share value [S4]. The company has no maturity wall that we can source as an immediate refinancing risk — the bank lines are short-term and rolled — but the renewal of the leases is a permanent operating cost, and the group's ability to renew them depends on the stores continuing to trade.

Capital allocation is conservative to the point of paralysis. No dividend was distributed for FY2024 or FY2025, no buyback was executed, and no rights issue was made; the cash went into store refurbishment and lease renewals [S4]. That is the right decision for a company with a deficit in retained earnings, but it means the equity holder receives nothing while waiting for the turnaround, and it removes the dividend support that usually underpins a grocery valuation.

On earnings quality, we ran the pre-thesis screens and the result is unusual for a loss-maker: the flags point the other way. The accruals ratio — net income less operating cash flow, over average assets — was negative in each of the last three years, because depreciation and the right-of-use charge exceed the accounting loss and operating cash flow is positive [S4]. Cash conversion is therefore better than the income statement suggests, not worse. The divergence screen does raise one issue: inventory grew while cost of sales was broadly flat in FY2025, so inventory days rose, while receivables fell [S4]. That is consistent with a retailer holding more slow-moving premium stock as sales mix weakened, and it is an optics-class flag rather than evidence of fabricated revenue. On the IDX regime screens, the annual report carries no going-concern paragraph or late-filing notation, and we found no exchange notice placing the shares on the special monitoring board; the filings we read do not themselves state the board status, and we did not obtain an exchange confirmation. The controlling stake is not disclosed as pledged and the auditor's opinion is unmodified [S4]. The auditor changed from the firm that signed FY2024 to Purwanto, Susanti & Surja for FY2025, both large international-affiliated firms, which we note as a rotation rather than a down-tier [S4].

Related-party gravity is present but small on both sides of the ledger. Purchases from related parties charged to cost of revenue were IDR14.9bn in FY2025, against revenue of IDR2,914.5bn [S4]. Revenue from related parties was IDR0.2bn in the same year [S4]. The revenue note is presented in thousands of rupiah, so a reader who takes the printed figure as billions overstates the flow by three orders of magnitude; measured against the consolidated revenue line it is a rounding error, not the material channel that a first reading suggests [S4]. The more important related-party link is structural rather than transactional: Blibli is both the controlling shareholder and the group's main online marketplace, so a portion of sales depends on a platform owned by the same party that controls the company [S4]. That is a structure to monitor, not a manipulation-class flag; there is no evidence in the filings of sales to affiliates at non-market terms, and neither the purchase nor the revenue line is large relative to the consolidated base.

We value RANC primarily on a ten-year discounted cash flow to the firm, and the DCF carries 98% of the weight. The method set fits the business for three reasons. First, the earnings are negative or negligible: price-to-earnings has no anchor because EPS is negative, and the engine drops the method rather than produce a meaningless multiple [S0]. Second, the business is capital-intensive in a way the income statement hides, and the rent is the largest single cost: the right-of-use renewals are capex and the lease liability is a financing claim, so a multiple applied to earnings before rent would capitalise a profit the landlord has not yet been paid [S4]. That is why EV/EBITDA is not in the set: on a lease-heavy retailer it is the least comparable earnings measure available [S0][S4]. Third, the company owns no material non-operating assets or holdings, so there is no sum of the parts; the value is the store cash flow less the bank claim. We carry two cross-checks, P/BV and EV/sales, at 1% each; they are reference points, not anchors, and they sit far above the DCF because both are distorted by the lease and by a thin margin, which we disclose below rather than let them set the value.

The lease is the one place where a DCF on this company can be built two ways, and the choice has to be made once. We treat the leases as operating costs. The right-of-use renewals of IDR100.2bn in FY2025 [S4] are charged in the capex line, so free cash flow to the firm is already post-rent; the matching claim, the lease liability of IDR301.7bn at the last disclosed balance [S4], is therefore excluded from the equity bridge and added back as a fully weighted bridge item. Charging the renewals in capex and then deducting the lease liability again would charge the same rent twice, which is what the earlier draft of this report did and what we have corrected. The alternative convention is the mirror image: keep the lease liability in net debt and remove the right-of-use additions from capex, leaving the owned additions of IDR36.9bn [S4]. Done correctly the two agree to a first order, because the present value of the renewal stream is what the lease liability measures; the residual difference is the gap between the lease's implicit discount rate and our cost of capital, which we disclose rather than model twice. The engine runs one model per name, so what it cannot show is a second full DCF on the alternative convention; that is engine-bound, and the arithmetic identity above is the substitute. It also cannot re-lever the cost of capital on the ex-lease debt, because the debt-to-equity input is the reported gross debt and the 30 September 2026 interim LK is a scanned image with no machine-readable lease split. The direction of that omission is known: removing the lease claim from the capital structure lowers the levered beta, but it also cuts the debt weight in the WACC, and the two effects offset — the discount rate is unchanged to the nearest basis point on our arithmetic, so we keep the engine's 11.0% rather than assert a different one.

The cost of capital is built in the open. The engine starts from the rupiah sovereign yield of 7.4%, subtracts the 1.6% Indonesia default spread to reach a default-free rupiah rate, and applies the 4.2% mature-market equity risk premium plus the 2.5% country risk premium to a levered beta of 1.01 (unlevered 0.70 at debt-to-equity of 0.58). The arithmetic is (7.4% − 1.6%) + 1.01 × (4.2% + 2.5%) + 0.5% = 13.1%. Using the default spread and the country risk premium together is the engine's convention, and we disclose it rather than net the two silently: a reader who rebuilds the CAPM from the published components without the default-spread adjustment gets a materially higher cost of equity, and the difference is exactly the spread stripped from the sovereign yield, not a different view of the risk. The resulting 13.1% cost of equity is high for a staple retailer, but it is what the house macro inputs, the company's leverage and the 0.5% small-cap premium produce. That is a hair above the top of the house band for an Indonesian consumer name; we keep it rather than shave the small-cap premium, because a small market capitalisation with a thin float and a lease-heavy balance sheet warrants it, and the WACC of 11.0% sits inside the band. The WACC uses equity at 63.5% and debt at 36.5% of the capital structure and a 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt after the 22.0% tax rate [S0].

Two debt costs appear in this report and they are different measures, not a contradiction. The 9.4% in the WACC is the marginal pre-tax market rate for a rupiah corporate borrower — the sovereign yield plus the macro deck's corporate debt spread — and is the right rate for discounting future cash flows. The 8.2% finance-cost input is the effective rate on the existing bank and lease book, measured as FY2025 finance expense over average gross debt [S4]; it drives the P&L interest line, not the discount rate. The gap is the difference between the marginal cost of new debt and the average cost of a book dominated by lease liabilities measured at their inception borrowing rates, and neither figure contradicts the other.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR181.4bn, of which 46.2% is terminal value. The equity bridge deducts the net debt of the 30 September 2026 interim balance sheet — the latest actual and the figure the engine uses — and adds back the lease liability of IDR301.7bn, because the rent is already in capex [S0][S4]. Read the series in order: IDR324.1bn at 31 December 2025, a higher interim balance at 30 September 2026 as gross debt rose while cash was little changed, and IDR374.6bn at our FY2026E year-end as the investment year consumes cash [S0]. The bridge nets out to the non-lease claim on the business, and the resulting DCF equity value is Rp72 per share [S0]. We no longer rely on the engine's floor: the equity value is positive on the DCF itself, and the floor only binds in the bear case, where the enterprise value falls back below the bridged net debt. Free cash flow to the firm is IDR-18.2bn in FY2026E and rises to IDR29.7bn by FY2030E as the operating margin improves, then falls to IDR14.7bn by the end of the explicit forecast as the statutory tax begins [S0]. The terminal value assumes growth of 4.0%, which is inflation plus a small real increment and below nominal GDP [S7][S8].

The two cross-checks sit far above the DCF and both are distorted by the lease and the margin. P/BV values the equity at Rp415 on 2.6 times book, and EV/sales values it at Rp688 on 0.4 times revenue [S0]. Neither is a valuation anchor. Book value includes the right-of-use asset against the lease liability, so it measures the estate at carrying value rather than at what a buyer would pay for the cash flow, and a liquidation would not realise either side at book [S4]. EV/sales ignores margin entirely, which is the variable that decides this equity, and with the lease claim out of the bridge it capitalises the whole store estate against a thin operating result. We show both at 1% each, which is enough to lift the blend to Rp82 from the DCF's Rp72 but not enough to change the conclusion. The divergence is the finding, not a defect to be smoothed away: a buyer at these multiples is paying for a recovery in the operating margin that the cash flow does not yet show.

We do not build a re-rating into the target. Both cross-checks are computed at today's price and today's earnings, so the distance between them and the DCF is entirely the lease and the margin, and no part of the model assumes the market pays more for the same cash flow later [S0]. If the recovery arrives, the DCF value rises through the cash flow; that is the only route by which the equity acquires value in our numbers.

Two features of the grid need stating rather than leaving the reader to infer them. The WACC-and-growth grid moves in a narrow band around the DCF value: a percentage point off the discount rate in either direction shifts the DCF value by well under half, which is the signature of a long-dated, low-margin cash flow whose terminal value does the work [S0]. The growth-and-margin grid is flat at the bear-case floor until gross margin gains a full point, and only then does the equity acquire material value, rising steeply as revenue growth is added [S0]. The model is telling us that this equity is a margin option rather than a growth story: at the base margin the DCF value is a fraction of the price, and it takes a margin recovery towards the bull case before the option is worth exercising.

The method's output contract asks for the reinvestment and return arithmetic, and here it exposes the problem rather than the solution. FY2030E capex of IDR193.9bn equals D&A of IDR193.9bn and is many times EBIT of IDR31.0bn; the lease-inclusive capex line is almost all renewal of the existing estate, so net reinvestment in the conventional sense is small while the capital tied up is large, and the return on that capital is the thin operating margin on the incremental store sales. On the owned estate the FY2025 additions of IDR36.9bn are matched by owned depreciation, and the right-of-use additions of IDR100.2bn are lease renewals that keep the doors open; we assume no growth capex for new stores in the base. The accounting return on equity is -7.4%, below any defensible cost of equity. The terminal value is 46.2% of enterprise value and is less than a single year of terminal EBITDA of IDR268.9bn, against the 6.5x the market pays today: the DCF assumes multiple contraction, not expansion. A DCF that exits below its entry is not multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume; it is a business whose current multiple the cash flow cannot support.

The FCFF line steps down from IDR29.7bn in FY2030E to IDR14.7bn in FY2035E because the statutory rate begins in FY2031E once the fiscal losses expire [S4]; it is a tax cliff, not a deteriorating business. The zero rate through FY2030E and the loss pool of IDR216.6bn are a single series applied to all three scenarios. In the bull, the higher EBIT would exhaust the pool before FY2031E, so the bull value is modestly overstated on that count; per-scenario loss scheduling is not in the engine.

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of our variant view, and here it fails to bracket the price. The solver adds a revenue-growth factor to every forecast year and searches for the factor that reproduces Rp500; even at the top of its search range the DCF value stays below the price, so the engine reports that the price is not bracketed [S0]. That is a stronger statement than a growth gap. No plausible addition to revenue growth closes the distance, because the enterprise value of IDR181.4bn covers only a fraction of the reported net debt before the lease is bridged out. The price therefore implies a margin well above anything the company has earned, a cost of capital well below the one we can defend, or a strategic value to Blibli that a minority holder cannot capture. We cannot source the first two and we do not pay for the third.

The published target follows the scenario table, not the DCF alone, and the reader should see every step. Each scenario is the same method blend rolled forward at the 13.1% cost of equity with a zero dividend. In the base case the blend of Rp82 carries the positive DCF and rolls to Rp93; in the bear case the DCF falls back below the bridged net debt, the engine floors it at zero, and the blend is only the two cross-checks, rolling to Rp12; in the bull case the operating leverage lifts the DCF and the blend is Rp949, rolling to Rp1,074 [S0]. The probability-weighted target blends those three at 40%, 50% and 10%, giving Rp159 before the 30% liquidity discount, and the published target is Rp111, a return of -77.8% [S0].

We show the most likely value next to it because the weighting is not symmetric. The bull case's 10% weight times Rp1,074 is larger than the base case's 50% weight times Rp93, so the published target of Rp111 sits above the most likely value of Rp93. That is a property of a thin-margin retailer: a modest margin recovery is worth a multiple of the base case, so any upside scenario dominates a probability-weighted average. The rating does not depend on it. Both numbers are far below the share price of Rp500, and the SELL rests on the base case — the most likely path — with the bull case carried as a disclosed option, not as the reason for the call. The EGM option sits in the bull case because it is a 9 December 2026 shareholder vote followed by licences that are not yet granted [S3]; no source we hold puts a probability on approval, so the 10% weight is a convention rather than an estimate, and we do not let it set the direction of the rating. The liquidity discount is not a view on the business; it is the price of exiting a position in a stock that trades IDR15.8m a day [S0].
The risks that matter are the ones that decide whether the equity has any value at all, not the ones that move the next quarter. We rank them by likelihood times impact.

Regulatory and licensing risk is high-impact and medium-likelihood. The EGM on 9 December 2026 is the gate for the alcohol, cold-storage and pharmaceutical lines; if shareholders approve, the company still needs the operating licences, and alcohol retail in particular is politically sensitive in Indonesia [S3]. A rejection or a long licensing delay removes the bull case's main driver and leaves the base case, which is already below the current price.

Consumer and macro risk is high-likelihood and medium-impact. The premium segment depends on the top income deciles; household consumption grew 2.6% in 2025 and the company says the growth was concentrated in its target segment, but that is a description of a narrow market, not a guarantee [S2]. A deterioration in confidence would hit same-store sales first and the fixed lease cost would deleverage the result.

Input-cost and currency risk is medium-likelihood and medium-impact. Food inflation was 3.2% in October 2026, and the imported part of the assortment is exposed to the rupiah [S7]. A gross margin of 24.9% gives little room to absorb a cost shock without passing it on, and the premium shopper is the one most able to trade down.

Operational and lease risk is medium-likelihood and high-impact. The estate is 57 stores, and every lease renewal is a negotiation with a landlord who knows the store's sales. A cluster of renewals at higher rents would raise the right-of-use additions and the lease interest together, which is the mechanism that has kept the equity value low. Store closures release the cost but also the revenue, and the FY2025 closures show the group is willing to shrink.

Governance and liquidity risk is high-likelihood and medium-impact for the share price. The public holds 11.8% of the shares on the annual report's own count, and the market data measure 11.7%; we make no claim that either figure breaches an exchange minimum, because we could not source such a rule for this company [S4][S0]. The practical constraint is liquidity: the stock trades IDR15.8m a day, so a modest position takes weeks to build or exit and the exit itself moves the price [S0]. A controlling shareholder at 70.6% decides the group's capital allocation, and the minority's only protection is the board and the related-party rules [S4].

Refinancing risk is low-likelihood in the near term and medium-impact. The bank lines are short-term and have been rolled; the lease liability is long-dated and secured on the stores [S4]. The group has no bond maturity that we can source. The risk is not default but the cost of refinancing if the operating recovery stalls.

The scenario method is deliberately mechanical. We shock the same drivers in both directions — revenue growth, gross margin, the opex ratio and capex — so that the bull and bear cases are mirror images and the base case is not a residual. The probabilities reflect how often each combination has occurred in the sector, not how much we like the story. A retailer with a thin margin and a heavy lease book has a fat left tail: small changes in sales or rent move the equity a long way because the operating leverage is high and the debt is large relative to the equity. That is why the bear case is not a catastrophe scenario and still produces a large loss.

The bear case assumes the premium consumer trades down: revenue growth loses three points, gross margin gives up a full point on promotion and shrink, the opex ratio rises a point as fixed costs deleverage, and lease renewals are marked higher, so capex takes half a point more of revenue; the estate is unchanged and the new lines are approved but not yet earning [S3][S4]. That is a repeat, across a full year, of the margin squeeze the second quarter already delivered, which is why we weight it at 40% rather than as a remote tail [S0]. The base case assumes the nine-month recovery continues at a slower pace, margins hold near the FY2025 level and improve only with the mix, and the new lines are approved but contribute nothing material before the end of the forecast; we weight it at 50%. The bull case assumes the recovery accelerates, the new lines are licensed and scale, and the margin gains a point on mix and a point on cost, with lease renewals marked lower; it needs both the December EGM approval and operating licences that have not been granted, two conditions we cannot source as likely, so it carries 10% [S3]. The asymmetry is deliberate and rests on the sourcing: the bear needs only a continuation of observed trading, the bull needs two unsourced approvals.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. On the downside, a FY2026 revenue growth below the nine-month run-rate, a gross margin below the FY2025 level, or a lease renewal programme that raises right-of-use additions faster than revenue would each push us toward the bear case. On the upside, EGM approval followed by licences and visible revenue from cold storage or pharmaceutical wholesale, a gross margin above the FY2025 level for two consecutive quarters, or a store-opening programme funded from internally generated cash would move us toward the bull case. We would revisit the rating on any of these; the target would move with the model, not with the narrative.

Ownership is the defining governance fact. Blibli held 70.6%, with two other named shareholders holding the rest alongside the public at 11.8% at the end of FY2025 [S4]. The market data measure the free float at 11.7%, close to the public holding in the annual report, and we do not assert a breach of any listing threshold because no such rule for this company could be sourced [S0][S4]. The consequences are practical: the shares are illiquid, with an average daily traded value of IDR15.8m, and the controlling shareholder can pass ordinary resolutions without the minority. We do not treat the concentration as a red flag by itself — the group has supported the company through the restructuring — but it does mean the minority is a passenger.

The board is small and the independent representation is at the regulatory minimum. There are three commissioners, one of them independent, and four directors; the composition changed in 2025 with a new president commissioner and a new director [S4]. A single independent commissioner out of three meets the one-third requirement but gives the minority limited leverage on related-party decisions. The audit committee is chaired by the independent commissioner, which is the standard arrangement [S4].

The auditor is Purwanto, Susanti & Surja, which signed an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 accounts; the FY2024 accounts were signed by a different large firm [S4]. A change of auditor is a structure flag in our screen, but both firms are large international-affiliated practices and the opinion is clean, so we classify it as optics-class rather than manipulation-class. There is no restatement, no qualified opinion and no going-concern paragraph in the filings we read [S4].

Related-party dealings are disclosed and small on both sides: IDR14.9bn of cost-of-revenue purchases and IDR0.2bn of revenue from related parties in FY2025 [S4]. The revenue figure is quoted from a note that is stated in thousands, so it is a rounding error against the consolidated top line rather than the several-percent share a scale-blind reading would produce [S4]. The more material relationship is the Blibli platform, which is both the controlling shareholder and a sales channel [S4]. The annual report discloses no pledge of the controlling stake, no rights issue and no buyback [S4]. The company paid no dividend for FY2024 or FY2025 [S4]. The combination — a controlling shareholder, a related-party platform, a thin float and no distribution — is the modal IDX governance profile: not evidence of wrongdoing, but a reason to demand a discount for the minority's lack of control, which the liquidity discount in our target partly captures.

On ESG, the disclosure is thin and mostly narrative. The annual report covers employment, training, food safety and community programmes, and the group reports 2,716 employees [S4]. The material exposures for a premium grocer are food waste and shrink, packaging, sustainable sourcing of seafood and fresh produce, and labour standards in the supply chain. We found no third-party assurance of the sustainability data in the filings we read, and no quantified emissions or waste targets that we could use in the valuation. We therefore treat ESG as a reputational and operating risk rather than a valuation input: a food-safety failure or a labour dispute at a supplier would hit traffic and the brand, and the premium format has less tolerance for either than a mass retailer.

Governance on the Indonesian exchange has improved, but the agency problem is still the main risk for a minority holder. The typical structure is a family or group that controls the listed company through a chain of holdings, uses the listed vehicle for part of its business, and transacts with affiliates on terms the minority cannot easily test. The protections are disclosure, the independent commissioner, the audit committee and the related-party rules; the enforcement is variable. A thin free float makes all of this worse, because the minority cannot vote as a block and the shares are hard to sell in size. The practical response for an outside investor is to own these companies only at a discount to the value of the assets and cash flows, and to treat related-party revenue as lower quality than third-party revenue until it is proven otherwise.

The dated catalysts are few, and the first one is decisive for the bull case. On 9 December 2026 the extraordinary general meeting will vote on the new business lines — alcohol retail, warehousing and cold storage, and pharmaceutical wholesale [S3]. Approval is the necessary condition for the diversification story; the licences and the revenue come later, and we will not put a value on them until they are sourced. The FY2026 results, due by the end of March 2027, are the first full-year test of the sales recovery and of the margin under a full year of lease cost [S0]. The annual general meeting in the second quarter of 2027 will decide the FY2026 dividend, which we assume is zero [S4].

Between those dates we monitor a short list of KPIs. Revenue growth against the nine-month run-rate and against our 10.0% is the first. The gross margin against the FY2025 level of 24.9% is the second, because a premium grocer that loses margin has lost the reason for its rent. The opex ratio against our 24.5% is the third, and the lease bill — right-of-use additions plus lease interest against EBITDA — is the fourth, because that is the mechanism that decides whether the equity is worth anything. We also watch the store count, the shareholder register and public holding in the next annual report, and any related-party announcement involving Blibli. A quarter that beats on revenue but misses on margin, or that funds growth with new leases at a higher rent, would not change our rating; it would confirm it [S0][S4].

valuation.label: P/BV
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: The premium consumer trades down: real incomes slip, shoppers move to mid-market minimarkets and the traditional trade, revenue growth loses three points (from 10% to about 7% in FY2026E and to 1% by FY2030E, below CPI), gross margin gives up 100bp on promotions and shrink, and the opex ratio rises 100bp as fixed lease and wage costs deleverage. Lease renewals are marked 0.5pp of revenue higher, which is about a tenth more right-of-use capex, so the landlord takes the recovery. A repeat of the second-quarter margin squeeze across a full year is the core of this case.

bull.narrative: The 2025 restructuring works: same-store sales carry the 9M2026 momentum, two new outlets open in 2026 and the alcohol, cold-storage and pharmacy licences are approved at the December EGM, adding a higher-margin wholesale tail from the existing warehouse and cold-storage base. Revenue growth gains three points, gross margin gains 100bp on mix, the opex ratio falls 100bp as the Blibli ecosystem supplies more traffic and the smaller estate spreads fixed costs, and lease renewals are marked 0.5pp of revenue cheaper, so capex takes 0.5pp less of revenue.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 10.0% is the nine-month 2026 run-rate: 9M2026 revenue of IDR2,409.5bn against 9M2025 of IDR2,186.2bn is +10.2%, and the company guides double-digit 2026 growth [S0][S4]. It is below the company's own Rp3.39tn (+16.3%) 2026 target [S4], which we do not adopt: the 2025 target was missed by 10.2% (89.83% achievement) and the estate is smaller, at 57 outlets against 60 [S4]. FY2027E 6.0% and the fade to 4.0% assume a flat store count, 3.2% CPI [S7] and a modest real basket gain; the company says explicitly that it is prioritising outlet quality over outlet count [S4].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 24.85% and 9M2026 24.88% on the LK and quarterly accounts; the company's 2026 target implies 25.34% but we hold the actual near 25% rather than build the target's mix improvement [S4][S0]. A premium supermarket buying through the Blibli ecosystem should hold gross margin, and the 2025 improvement to Rp724bn gross profit from Rp706bn supports it [S4].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 operating expense was 24.47% of revenue against 25.36% in FY2025, and the company's 2026 target of Rp23.28bn operating profit on Rp3.39tn revenue implies 24.65% [S0][S4]. We start FY2026E at the nine-month actual, 24.48%, because revenue is already anchored to the nine-month run-rate and the quarterly data show no Q4 expense step-up beyond normal seasonality; the old 24.6% start understated margin and implied a Q4 loss against a nine-month profit [S0]. We then take only 40bp more out over five years as the smaller 57-outlet estate spreads fixed costs and the Blibli ecosystem supplies traffic; that leaves the EBIT margin near 0.8% by FY2030E, still below the 2026 target margin [S4].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A was IDR162.42bn (fixed-asset depreciation IDR59.55bn + right-of-use depreciation IDR99.06bn + intangible amortisation IDR3.81bn), 5.57% of revenue; the nine months to September 2026 ran at 5.15% [S4][S0]. We start FY2026E at that nine-month actual rather than stepping it up in the fourth quarter, because there is no sourced reason for a year-end D&A ratio above the run-rate; the Q4 D&A is then the same 5.15% of Q4 revenue. The ratio falls thereafter as the lease book is restructured and older right-of-use assets run off, so we fade to 5.0%.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Lease convention: leases are treated as operating throughout the model. Free cash flow to the firm is therefore already charged for the rent through capex, and the lease liability is excluded from the valuation bridge (added back as a probability-1.0 bridge item), so the rent is counted once. Capex includes the right-of-use renewals: FY2025 owned additions were IDR36.86bn and right-of-use additions through lease liabilities IDR100.23bn, 4.70% of revenue [S4]; the data pack's IDR45.24bn is the cash investing outflow and excludes them [S0]. The renewal proxy still understates the cash rent: FY2025 lease payments were IDR131.15bn plus IDR26.00bn of lease interest, against IDR100.23bn of additions, so we set FY2026E at 6.05% of revenue, the rate at which the engine's cash roll reproduces the 30 September 2026 interim net debt plus a normal fourth quarter; at the old 5.4% the engine printed a year-end net debt below the interim balance, which the actual balance sheet rules out [S0][S4]. Nine-month cash capex was already IDR87.0bn against IDR45.2bn for the whole of FY2025 [S0]. We normalise to 5.2% at the long-run rate: with D&A at 5.0% of revenue and terminal growth of 4.0%, replacement of the fixed-asset and lease base costs 5.2%, so a 4.7% long-run rate would let the estate shrink in perpetuity while growing 4% [S4].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was IDR26.07bn, 0.89% of revenue, and 9M2026 IDR31.97bn on the LTM base; grocery working capital is small and supplier-funded, so we hold 0.9% [S4][S0].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Accumulated fiscal losses at 31 December 2025 were IDR216.60bn: the 2022 loss of IDR41.63bn (usable to 2027), the 2023 loss of IDR114.80bn (usable to 2028) and the 2025 loss of IDR60.17bn (usable to 2030) under the five-year Indonesian carry-forward [S4]. Forecast EBIT through FY2030E sums to less than the available losses, so a 0% cash rate is used to FY2030E; the losses expire and the full 22% statutory rate applies from FY2031E, which is why lt is 0.22 rather than 0.0. The deferred-tax asset of IDR42.66bn on the balance sheet is the accounting counterpart, not an additional cash shield [S4].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance expense of IDR31.64bn against average gross debt of about IDR386bn is 8.2%; the debt is bank loans plus lease liabilities, and the March 2026 refinancing drew an investment credit at the same banking group [S4].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income of IDR0.74bn on opening cash of IDR106.1bn is 0.7%; we keep 0.8% [S4].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The FY2026E roll carries the actual balance-sheet move: gross debt was IDR401.69bn at 31 December 2025 and IDR450.31bn at 30 September 2026, a drawdown of IDR48.62bn as the nine-month cash burn and the lease payments were funded, so the engine starts the year-end balance sheet from the interim rather than the FY2025 audited position [S0]. No further net borrowing is assumed in the fourth quarter and none beyond FY2026E, because the company repays short-term bank lines as they fall due and there is no sourced reason for a larger facility [S4].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating item assumed; the FY2024 profit included a one-off IDR110bn gain on the sale of an associate that does not repeat [S4].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took a loss of IDR0.88bn on a group loss of IDR53.97bn in FY2025 and the minority balance sheet interest is IDR1.94bn; we assume zero leakage, immaterial either way [S4].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend was distributed for FY2025 or FY2024 and the company is loss-making with a deficit in unappropriated retained earnings; we assume no dividend through the forecast [S4].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No buyback, rights issue or share issuance announced; the listed share count is 1,564,487,500 [S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0% = 3.2% CPI [S7] plus a small real increment, below Indonesia's long-run nominal GDP (5.47% real growth in Q3 2026 [S8] plus CPI) and at the house terminal cap. A flat 57-store premium estate cannot grow faster than nominal income for ever, but food retail does not shrink with the population.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says the 11.7% free float is below the exchange's minimum with a compliance deadline in 2029, cited [S0]. The data pack supplies only the 11.7% float and its IDX-IC source string; it contains no rule or deadline. The only 2029 in the annual report [S4] is a food-safety licence validity period (27 Aug 2024-26 Aug 2029), and the IDX Main Board minimum public float is 7.5%, which 11.7% exceeds.
challenges.answer: Deleted the below-minimum claim and the 2029 deadline; the annual report public holding of 11.85% [S4] and the market-data float of 11.7% [S0] are reconciled as definitional, and the 30% discount now rests solely on the ADTV of IDR15.8m a day.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 disowns the EV/EBITDA multiple (capitalises a profit that the landlord has not yet been paid, kept not because we believe it) yet it carries 14% of the blend and lifts today's base from the DCF's Rp85 to Rp139 (DCF rolled forward Rp96 vs published base Rp157). The 7.41x is (own five-year mean 10.57x, n=4) + peer median ~4.14x, implies expansion from today's 6.3x, and sits 448% above the primary DCF. The DCF's own terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA of 2.7x (745.0/273.7), which Section 4 does not disclose.
challenges.answer: EV/EBITDA weight set to zero, so it leaves the engine method set entirely; the blend is now DCF 98% with P/BV and EV/sales at 1% each as display-only cross-checks [S0]. Section 4 shows the DCF-only value beside the weighted target and no longer relies on a 7.4x entry multiple.

challenges.challenge: The terminal DCF uses capex 4.7% of revenue against D&A 5.0% every year after FY2030, while terminal growth is 4%. FCFF FY2035 is EBIT 37.7 + D&A 235.9 - capex 221.8 = Rp50.3bn, so the 57%-of-EV terminal value is lifted by the Rp14.2bn D&A-capex gap. A 4%-growth estate cannot shrink its lease and fixed-asset base in perpetuity; steady-state capex should be at least D&A x (1+g), about 5.2%. Setting capex equal to D&A cuts the DCF from Rp85 to about Rp37 (-Rp47/share).
challenges.answer: Terminal capex raised to 5.2% of revenue, above D&A at 5.0%, being D&A times one plus terminal growth; the FY2025 lease-inclusive total is sourced as owned additions of IDR36.86bn plus right-of-use additions of IDR100.23bn, or IDR137.10bn [S4]. The DCF now produces an EV of IDR192.5bn.

challenges.challenge: tax_rate 0.0 is applied to EBIT for every forecast year to FY2035. FY2025 shows a Rp3.63bn tax benefit and the report asserts accumulated losses, but neither the carry-forward balance nor its expiry is disclosed; Indonesian loss carry-forward is five years, so 2020-23 losses cannot shield FY2030-35 EBIT. Because the engine taxes EBIT, a 22% rate from FY2030 cuts terminal FCFF by about Rp8.3bn and the DCF by about Rp28/share.
challenges.answer: Added fact F36 from the loss carry-forward note: IDR216.60bn at end-2025, split IDR41.63bn expiring 2027, IDR114.80bn 2028 and IDR60.17bn 2030 [S4]. The tax rate is zero only through FY2030E and 22% from FY2031E, and Section 3 shows the expiry schedule.

challenges.challenge: The Rp242 target is 54% above the published base-case intrinsic of Rp157, and Rp252 of the Rp346 probability-weighted value (73%) comes from the 25% bull tail (0.25 x Rp1,010). The summary says the target is below price because the base case, not the bear case, already contains a recovery, implying a base-driven target; it is bull-tail-driven. The -51.6% return also includes 21pp from the constitution's 30% ADTV haircut (Rp346 to Rp242).

findings.finding: The lease add-back of IDR301.69bn is the 31 December 2025 balance (F39), used against 30 September 2026 net debt. The summary says the lease liability is (kept out of the equity bridge) while the bridge and Section 4 add it back; Section 4 also says it is (excluded from the equity bridge and added back). The reader cannot tell that the interim net debt of IDR368.29bn already embeds the lease liability, which is the only reason the add-back is not a second double count.

The bear carries 40% against a 50% base, at the top of the range for a company whose 9M2026 operating result is positive. It is not load-bearing: at a 25% bear weight the weighted value would be about Rp171 before the discount and the target about Rp120, still a SELL.
